Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

content.text:
`src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

goal.objective:
Finish the resolver in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ResolveError`, `parseVersion`, `compareVersions`, `parseRange`, `satisfies` and `maxSatisfying` from `src/semver.js` and `ConflictError` and `resolve` from `src/resolve.js`; keep that surface. `ResolveError` extends `Error`, sets `name` to `'ResolveError'`, carries a `code` and is constructed as `(code, message)`. A version is exactly three numeric parts with no leading zeros and no suffix; `parseVersion` returns `{ major, minor, patch }` and otherwise throws `'BAD_VERSION'` with message `invalid version: <text>`. `compareVersions(left, right)` returns -1, 0 or 1 by comparing the three parts numerically, so `1.10.0` is above `1.9.0`.

`parseRange(text)` turns a range into the list of comparators that must all hold, each `{ operator, version }` with an operator of `>=`, `<=`, `>`, `<` or `=`. Whitespace around the range is ignored and one or more spaces separate conjuncts. `*` alone means no comparators at all and may not appear beside anything else. A bare version, or one written with `=`, is an equality comparator. `^V` means at least `V` and below the next version that changes the leftmost non-zero part: `^1.2.3` spans up to but excluding `2.0.0`, `^0.2.3` up to `0.3.0`, and `^0.0.3` up to `0.0.4`. `~V` means at least `V` and below the next minor, so `~1.2.3` spans up to `1.3.0`. Anything else, including an empty range, a lone operator, an operator separated from its version by a space, or an unparseable version, throws `'BAD_RANGE'` with message `invalid range: <text>`. `satisfies(version, range)` tests one version against every comparator, and `maxSatisfying(versions, range)` returns the highest satisfying version of a list or null.

`resolve(registry, rootDeps)` picks exactly one version per package. The registry maps a package name to an object of versions, each version to metadata whose optional `deps` maps a package name to a range. It is validated up front: a non-object registry throws `'BAD_REGISTRY'` with message `registry must be an object`, a non-object package entry gives `registry entry must be an object: <name>`, every version key must parse, non-object metadata gives `metadata must be an object: <name>@<version>`, and a dependency map that is not an object throws `'BAD_DEPENDENCIES'` with message `dependencies of <name>@<version> must be an object`. The root map is validated the same way, with `root dependencies must be an object`, and every range in either place must parse.

Resolution keeps a list of constraints per package and a set of pending packages, seeded from the root dependencies taken in ascending name order, where each root constraint records the origin `<root>`. While anything is pending, take the lexicographically smallest pending name and select it: a name absent from the registry throws `'UNKNOWN_PACKAGE'` with message `unknown package: <name>`; otherwise the candidates are the registry's versions of that package that satisfy every constraint recorded for it so far, and the highest candidate wins. Selecting a package at a version gives it a chain, which is the origin recorded with its first constraint followed by ` > <name>@<version>`, so a root dependency `a` chosen at 1.0.0 has the chain `<root> > a@1.0.0`. Its dependencies are then walked in ascending name order: each adds a constraint whose origin is the selecting package's chain, and a dependency that has not been selected becomes pending, while one that is already selected must still satisfy the new range. A package with no satisfying candidate, and a selected package that a later constraint contradicts, both raise `ConflictError`, which extends `ResolveError`, sets `name` to `'ConflictError'` and `code` to `'CONFLICT'`, and carries `packageName`, `available` (that package's versions in ascending order) and `constraints`, the recorded constraints as `{ range, via }` in the order they arrived. Its message is `cannot satisfy <name>: ` followed by those constraints as `<range> (from <via>)` joined with `, `. On success the result is `{ resolved, order }`, where `resolved` maps names to versions in ascending name order and `order` lists the names in the order they were selected. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Validate up front. A count that is not a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `count must be a non-negative integer`. An element that is not a safe integer in `0 .. count - 1` raises `RangeError` with message `element out of range: 7`, quoting the offending value. An edge list that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `edges must be an array`, an edge that is not a three-element array raises `TypeError` with message `edge must be [u, v, weight]`, a weight that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `weight must be a finite number`, and an alternatives argument that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `alternatives must be an array`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. The operations are `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`. `add` creates or overwrites an object member, and inside an array it inserts before the given index, where the index may equal the length and the token `-` appends. `remove` and `replace` require an existing target, and `replace` on the empty pointer replaces the whole document while `remove` on it throws `cannot remove the whole document`. `move` removes the value at `from` and adds it at `path`, is a no-op when the two pointers are equal, and throws `cannot move a value into its own child` when `from` is a proper prefix of `path`. `copy` adds an independent copy of the value at `from`. `test` compares the value at `path` with `value` as JSON — object members in any order, array elements in order, and no type coercion — and throws `test failed at /a/y` when they differ.

Every failure from `applyPatch` is a `PatchError` whose `index` is the 0-based position of the operation that failed; when the cause was a pointer failure, the message is that failure's message and `cause` is the `PointerError`. Operations are checked before they run: a non-object operation throws `operation must be an object`, an unrecognised or missing `op` throws `unknown operation: frob`, and missing members throw `add requires a path`, `add requires a value` or `move requires a from`. A patch that is not an array throws `patch must be an array`, and data that is not JSON throws `document is not JSON data` or `value is not JSON data`. Keys that shadow `Object.prototype`, including `__proto__`, are ordinary own properties throughout: adding `/__proto__` must leave the result's prototype and every other object alone, and resolving `/toString` on an empty object must fail. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. 230:     const rightAssociative = node.op === '^';

232:     const rightPrecedence = precedenceOf(node.right);
233:     const left = (rightAssociative ? leftPrecedence <= level : leftPrecedence < level) ? `(${render(node.left)})` : render(node.left);

goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. `parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. `evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). Finish the ledger in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `ACCOUNT_TYPES`, `LedgerError`, `normalSide` and `toNormal` from `src/money.js` and `Ledger` from `src/ledger.js`; keep that surface. Every failure is a `LedgerError` (extending `Error`, `name` set to `'LedgerError'`, constructed as `(code, message)`) carrying a `code`. Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. 5: /** Deterministic 32-bit PRNG so generated postings replay identically. */
6: function mulberry32(seed) {
7:   let a = seed >>> 0;
8:   return function next() {
9:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
10:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
11:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
12:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
13:   };
14: }

16: /** A ledger with the five accounts used across these cases. */
17: function chartOfAccounts() {
18:   const ledger = new Ledger();
19:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'cash', name: 'Cash', type: 'asset' });
20:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'revenue', name: 'Revenue', type: 'income' });
21:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'ap', name: 'Payables', type: 'liability' });
22:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'rent', name: 'Rent', type: 'expense' });
23:   ledger.openAccount({ id: 'equity', name: 'Equity', type: 'equity' });
24:   return ledger;
25: }

27: /** The worked example used by the balance and reversal cases. */
28: function seeded() {
29:   const ledger = chartOfAccounts();
30:   ledger.post({ id: 'e1', at: 10, memo: 'sale', lines: [{ account: 'cash', amountCents: 1000 }, { account: 'revenue', amountCents: -1000 }] });
31:   ledger.post({ id: 'e2', at: 20, lines: [{ account: 'rent', amountCents: 300 }, { account: 'cash', amountCents: -300 }] });

Amounts are integer cents in one signed convention: a positive amount is a debit and a negative amount is a credit, so a balanced entry sums to zero. The account types are `asset`, `liability`, `equity`, `income` and `expense`; `normalSide(type)` returns `'debit'` for assets and expenses and `'credit'` for the other three, and `toNormal(type, signedCents)` negates the debit-positive figure for credit-normal types. Both throw `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` with message `unknown account type: <type>` for anything else.

`openAccount({ id, name, type })` registers an account and returns it frozen. It throws `'BAD_ACCOUNT'` with message `account must be an object` for a non-object, `account id must be a non-empty string` or `account name must be a non-empty string` for those fields, `'UNKNOWN_TYPE'` for an unknown type, and `'DUPLICATE_ACCOUNT'` with message `account already exists: <id>` for a repeat. `accounts()` lists the accounts in ascending id order.

`post({ id, at, memo, lines })` appends an immutable entry. Validation runs in this order, and nothing is stored unless every check passes: the entry must be an object (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry must be an object`); `id` must be a non-empty string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`, `entry id must be a non-empty string`) that has not been used (`'DUPLICATE_ENTRY'`, `entry already exists: <id>`); `at` must be a non-negative integer (`'BAD_TIME'`); `memo` defaults to the empty string and must be a string (`'BAD_ENTRY'`); `lines` must be an array of at least two lines (`'TOO_FEW_LINES'`); then each line in turn must name an account that exists (`'UNKNOWN_ACCOUNT'`, `unknown account: <id>`), carry a safe integer `amountCents` (`'NOT_INTEGER'`) that is not zero (`'ZERO_LINE'`); and finally the amounts must sum to zero (`'UNBALANCED'`). Entries may be posted in any time order.

`balance(accountId, { asOf })` sums the account's lines over the entries in force at that moment, keeping the debit-positive sign; `normalBalance` reports the same figure in the account's own direction. `trialBalance({ asOf })` returns `{ debits, credits, byAccount }` with every account present, `debits` the sum of the positive balances and `credits` the absolute sum of the negative ones; because entries balance, the two totals are always equal and the balances always sum to zero. `reverse(entryId, { id, at, memo })` posts the mirror image of an entry, negating every line, defaulting the memo to `reversal of <entryId>`, recording `reverses` on the new entry and `reversedBy` on the old one. `src/index.js` must export `parse`, `expand` and the error class `UriTemplateError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parse(template)` returns the template's parts in order: `{ type: 'literal', value }` for text outside braces, with adjacent literal text merged into one part, and `{ type: 'expression', operator, variables }` for each `{...}` group. `operator` is one of `+ # . / ; ? &` when the expression starts with it and the empty string otherwise. Each entry of `variables` is `{ name, explode, maxLength }`: `name*` sets `explode`, `name:3` sets `maxLength` to a number of 1 to 9999 written with no leading zero, and a name is one or more of letters, digits, `_` or a `%XX` triplet, with single dots allowed between them. An empty template yields no parts.

Parsing failures throw `UriTemplateError` whose `index` is the position of the `{` that opens the offending expression, or of the stray character: `unterminated expression at 1`, `unexpected '}' at 1`, `empty expression at 0`, `empty variable specification at 0`, `reserved operator '=' at 0` for the operators `= , ! @ |`, `invalid variable name 'a-b' at 0`, and `invalid prefix modifier ':0' at 0`. A non-string template throws `template must be a string`.

`expand(template, variables)` returns the expanded text. Literal parts keep unreserved characters, the reserved characters `:/?#[]@!$&'()*+,;=` and existing percent-triplets, and percent-encode everything else as uppercase UTF-8 triplets. Each expression looks its variables up as own properties of `variables`; a name that is absent, `null`, `undefined`, an array with no usable members or an object with no usable members contributes nothing, and `null` or `undefined` members inside an array or object are skipped. An expression whose variables all contribute nothing produces no text at all, not even its prefix. Otherwise the expression is its prefix followed by the pieces joined by its separator. The operators give (prefix, separator, named, empty-value text): the simple form (``, `,`, no, ``), `+` (``, `,`, no, ``), `#` (`#`, `,`, no, ``), `.` (`.`, `.`, no, ``), `/` (`/`, `/`, no, ``), `;` (`;`, `;`, yes, ``), `?` (`?`, `&`, yes, `=`) and `&` (`&`, `&`, yes, `=`). Values under `+` and `#` are encoded like literals; under every other operator only unreserved characters survive, so `/` becomes `%2F` and an existing `%20` becomes `%2520`.

A string, a finite number or a boolean expands to its text; anything else throws `value for 'a' is not a string, number or boolean`. Under a named operator a scalar becomes `name=value`, or `name` followed by the operator's empty-value text when the encoded value is empty. `:n` truncates a string to `n` characters, counted in code points and applied before encoding, and throws `prefix modifier applied to a composite value: 'dom'` for an array or object. An array without `*` joins its encoded items with `,` and, when named, becomes one `name=a,b` piece; with `*` each item is its own piece, named as `name=item`. An object without `*` flattens to `key,value,key,value` joined with `,` and behaves like an array otherwise; with `*` each pair is its own `key=value` piece, where a named operator applies the empty-value rule to a pair whose value is empty, and the keys are encoded like values. `variables` that is not an object throws `variables must be an object`. Finish `src/trie.js`, whose `Trie` class currently keeps words in a plain map. Build a real trie: one node per distinct prefix, walked by Unicode code point so a character outside the basic plane is a single step and never a pair of surrogate halves. Every listing is ordered by code point, so `'\uFF10'` comes before `'\uFFFD'` and both come before an emoji. You may add files under `src/`.

`insert(word, value)` stores a value and returns the value it replaced, or `undefined` when the word is new. `get(word)` and `has(word)` read it back. `delete(word)` removes a word, returns whether it removed one, and drops the nodes that word alone kept alive; deleting a string that is only a prefix of stored words removes nothing and returns `false`. `countPrefix(prefix)` returns how many stored words start with the prefix, and must cost the length of the prefix rather than a walk of the subtree, so keep a per-node count of the words below it. `search(prefix, limit)` lists the matching words in order, at most `limit` of them, defaulting to no limit; a prefix that is not in the index yields an empty list. `entries()` lists every `[word, value]` pair in order. `longestPrefixMatch(text)` returns `{ word, value }` for the longest stored word that is a prefix of `text`, or `null` when no stored word is.

The empty string is an ordinary word: it can be stored, it is a prefix of every string, and `countPrefix('')` is the number of stored words. `size` is the number of stored words. `nodeCount` counts nodes including the root, so an empty index has a node count of 1 and, after any sequence of inserts and deletes, the count equals the number of distinct prefixes of the stored words plus that root.

A word, prefix, or text argument that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `word must be a string`, `prefix must be a string`, or `text must be a string` respectively. A limit that is neither `Infinity` nor a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `limit must be a non-negative integer`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.

6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }
20: 
21: /**
22:  * Compares two strings by Unicode code point.
23:  * @param {string} a First string.
24:  * @param {string} b Second string.
25:  * @returns {number} Negative, zero, or positive.
26:  */
27: function byCodePoint(a, b) {
28:   const left = [...a];
29:   const right = [...b];
30:   for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(left.length, right.length); i += 1) {
31:     const diff = left[i].codePointAt(0) - right[i].codePointAt(0);
32:     if (diff !== 0) return diff;
33:   }
34:   return left.length - right.length;
35: }

37: /**
38:  * Every distinct prefix of a set of words, the empty prefix included.
39:  * @param {Iterable<string>} words Stored words.
40:  * @returns {Set<string>} Distinct prefixes.
41:  */
42: function prefixesOf(words) {
43:   const out = new Set(['']);
44:   for (const word of words) {
45:     const chars = [...word];
46:     for (let i = 1; i <= chars.length; i += 1) out.add(chars.slice(0, i).join(''));
47:   }
48:   return out;
49: }

`src/index.js` must export `parsePointer`, `formatPointer`, `resolve`, `applyPatch` and the error classes `PointerError` and `PatchError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `parsePointer(pointer)` turns pointer text into decoded reference tokens: the empty string is no tokens, and any other pointer must start with `/` and is split on every following `/`, so `'/'` is one empty token and `'//'` is two. Inside a token `~1` decodes to `/` and `~0` decodes to `~`, decoded left to right in one pass so `'/~01'` is the single token `~1`; a `~` followed by anything else throws `invalid escape in pointer token: ~2`. `formatPointer(tokens)` is the exact inverse, escaping `~` before `/`.

`resolve(document, pointer)` walks the document token by token and returns the selected value; the empty pointer returns the document itself. Inside an array a token must be `0` or a digit string with no leading zero, and it must be less than the length, otherwise `invalid array index: 01 at /list/01` or `index out of range: 3 at /list/3`. Inside an object the token must name an own property, otherwise `missing property: x at /a/x`. A token applied to a string, number, boolean or null throws `cannot index into string at /name/0`. Each of these carries the pointer up to and including the failing token, and every one is a `PointerError`.

`applyPatch(document, operations)` returns a new document with every operation applied. It never modifies its arguments and never shares structure with them: the document and every inserted value are deep-copied, so an empty patch still returns an independent copy. If any operation fails, the call throws and the document is left exactly as it was. 9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }
20: 
21: /**
22:  * Compares two strings by Unicode code point.
23:  * @param {string} a First string.
24:  * @param {string} b Second string.
25:  * @returns {number} Negative, zero, or positive.
26:  */
27: function byCodePoint(a, b) {
28:   const left = [...a];
29:   const right = [...b];
30:   for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(left.length, right.length); i += 1) {
31:     const diff = left[i].codePointAt(0) - right[i].codePointAt(0);
32:     if (diff !== 0) return diff;
33:   }
34:   return left.length - right.length;
35: }
36: 
37: /**
38:  * Every distinct prefix of a set of words, the empty prefix included.
39:  * @param {Iterable<string>} words Stored words.
40:  * @returns {Set<string>} Distinct prefixes.
41:  */
42: function prefixesOf(words) {
43:   const out = new Set(['']);
44:   for (const word of words) {
45:     const chars = [...word];
46:     for (let i = 1; i <= chars.length; i += 1) out.add(chars.slice(0, i).join(''));
47:   }
48:   return out;
49: }

goal.objective:
Finish `src/trie.js`, whose `Trie` class currently keeps words in a plain map. Build a real trie: one node per distinct prefix, walked by Unicode code point so a character outside the basic plane is a single step and never a pair of surrogate halves. Every listing is ordered by code point, so `'\uFF10'` comes before `'\uFFFD'` and both come before an emoji. You may add files under `src/`.

`insert(word, value)` stores a value and returns the value it replaced, or `undefined` when the word is new. `get(word)` and `has(word)` read it back. `delete(word)` removes a word, returns whether it removed one, and drops the nodes that word alone kept alive; deleting a string that is only a prefix of stored words removes nothing and returns `false`. `countPrefix(prefix)` returns how many stored words start with the prefix, and must cost the length of the prefix rather than a walk of the subtree, so keep a per-node count of the words below it. `search(prefix, limit)` lists the matching words in order, at most `limit` of them, defaulting to no limit; a prefix that is not in the index yields an empty list. `entries()` lists every `[word, value]` pair in order. `longestPrefixMatch(text)` returns `{ word, value }` for the longest stored word that is a prefix of `text`, or `null` when no stored word is.

The empty string is an ordinary word: it can be stored, it is a prefix of every string, and `countPrefix('')` is the number of stored words. `size` is the number of stored words. `nodeCount` counts nodes including the root, so an empty index has a node count of 1 and, after any sequence of inserts and deletes, the count equals the number of distinct prefixes of the stored words plus that root.

A word, prefix, or text argument that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `word must be a string`, `prefix must be a string`, or `text must be a string` respectively. A limit that is neither `Infinity` nor a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `limit must be a non-negative integer`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. Finish `src/dsu.js` and `src/kruskal.js`. `DisjointSets` holds the elements `0 .. count - 1` and joins them by size; the starting point can join and query, but it keeps no history, so `checkpoint`, `undo`, and `rollback` are unimplemented. `union(a, b)` attaches the smaller set's root under the larger set's root, and on a tie attaches the larger root index under the smaller one, returning `false` when both elements already shared a set. `find(element)` returns the representative of an element's set, `connected(a, b)` compares representatives, `sizeOf(element)` returns the size of an element's set, `components` counts the sets, and `count` is the number of elements. `groups()` lists the sets, each ascending, ordered by their smallest member.

The history is exact. `checkpoint()` returns a token naming the current state — the number of unions performed so far. `undo()` reverses the most recent union and returns `false` when there is none left. `rollback(token)` undoes unions until the state matches that checkpoint and returns how many it undid. After a rollback the structure must be indistinguishable from the moment the checkpoint was taken: the same partition, the same set sizes, and the same representative returned by `find` for every element. Because tokens count unions, they are naturally used newest-first: a token that has already been rolled past no longer names a reachable state. A token that is not a safe integer in `0 .. unions performed` raises `RangeError` with message `unknown checkpoint: 5`, quoting the token.

`src/kruskal.js` exports two functions over edges written `[u, v, weight]`. `minimumSpanningForest(count, edges)` takes the edges in weight order, breaking ties by first endpoint and then second endpoint, keeps an edge when it joins two different sets, and returns `{ edges, weight, components }` with the chosen edges in the order they were taken, their total weight, and how many components remain. `componentsWithAlternatives(count, baseEdges, alternatives)` applies the base edges once, then measures each alternative edge list on top of that base independently, rolling back between them, and returns `{ base, alternatives }` where `base` is the component count after the base edges and `alternatives` holds one component count per alternative.

Validate up front. A count that is not a non-negative safe integer raises `TypeError` with message `count must be a non-negative integer`. An element that is not a safe integer in `0 .. count - 1` raises `RangeError` with message `element out of range: 7`, quoting the offending value. An edge list that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `edges must be an array`, an edge that is not a three-element array raises `TypeError` with message `edge must be [u, v, weight]`, a weight that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `weight must be a finite number`, and an alternatives argument that is not an array raises `TypeError` with message `alternatives must be an array`. Do not add dependencies; `test/` and `package.json` are fixed and the suite must pass with `node --test test/*.test.js`. Change only files under src/. 1: /**
2:  * Disjoint sets over the elements `0 .. count - 1`, joined by size and undone
3:  * in reverse order.
4:  *
5:  * This starting point joins and queries sets but records nothing, so none of
6:  * the history operations work yet.
7:  */
8: export class DisjointSets {
9:   #parent;
10:   #size;
11:   #components;
12: 
13:   /**
14:    * @param {number} count How many elements the structure holds.
15:    */
16:   constructor(count) {
17:     this.#parent = Array.from({ length: count }, (_, index) => index);
18:     this.#size = new Array(count).fill(1);
19:     this.#components = count;
20:   }
21: 
22:   /** @returns {number} How many elements the structure holds. */
23:   get count() {
24:     return this.#parent.length;
25:   }
26: 
27:   /** @returns {number} How many disjoint sets exist right now. */
28:   get components() {
29:     return this.#components;
30:   }
31: 
32:   /**
33:    * Finds the representative of an element's set.
34:    * @param {number} element Element to look up.
35:    * @returns {number} Root element of the set.
36:    */
37:   find(element) {
38:     let node = element;
39:     while (this.#parent[node] !== node) node = this.#parent[node];
40:     for (let step = element; this.#parent[step] !== node; ) {
41:       const next = this.#parent[step];
42:       this.#parent[step] = node;
43:       step = next;
44:     }
45:     return node;
46:   }
47: 
48:   /**
49:    * Reports whether two elements share a set.
50:    * @param {number} a First element.
51:    * @param {number} b Second element.
52:    * @returns {boolean} True when both share a representative.
53:    */
54:   connected(a, b) {
55:     return this.find(a) === this.find(b);
56:   }
57: 
58:   /**
59:    * Reports how many elements share an element's set.
60:    * @param {number} element Element to measure.
61:    * @returns {number} Size of the set.
62:    */
63:   sizeOf(element) {
64:     return this.#size[this.find(element)];
65:   }
66: 
67:   /**
68:    * Joins two sets, attaching the smaller under the larger and, on a tie, the
69:    * larger root index under the smaller.
70:    * @param {number} a First element.
71:    * @param {number} b Second element.
72:    * @returns {boolean} False when both elements already shared a set.
73:    */
74:   union(a, b) {
75:     const rootA = this.find(a);
76:     const rootB = this.find(b);
77:     if (rootA === rootB) return false;
78:     const root = this.#size[rootB] > this.#size[rootA] ? rootB : rootA;
79:     const attached = root === rootA ? rootB : rootA;
80:     this.#parent[attached] = root;
81:     this.#size[root] += this.#size[attached];
82:     this.#components -= 1;
83:     return true;
84:   }

113:    * @returns {number[][]} Current partition.

6: /**
7:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.
8:  * @param {number} seed Initial state.
9:  * @returns {() => number} Generator returning floats in [0, 1).
10:  */
11: function mulberry32(seed) {
12:   let a = seed >>> 0;
13:   return () => {
14:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
15:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
16:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
17:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
18:   };
19: }

21: /**

23:  * @param {number[]} labels One label per element.
24:  * @returns {number[][]} Sets, each ascending, ordered by smallest member.
25:  */
26: function groupsOf(labels) {
27:   const byLabel = new Map();
28:   labels.forEach((label, element) => {
29:     if (!byLabel.has(label)) byLabel.set(label, []);
30:     byLabel.get(label).push(element);
31:   });
32:   return [...byLabel.values()].sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);

113: test('matches a snapshot model across random unions, checkpoints, and rollbacks', () => {
114:   const rnd = mulberry32(0x0f5e7);
115:   const size = 12;
116:   const sets = new DisjointSets(size);
117:   let labels = Array.from({ length: size }, (_, index) => index);
118:   /** @type {number[][]} */
119:   const history = [labels.slice()];
120:   /** @type {number[]} */
121:   const marks = [];
122:   let unions = 0;
123:   const totals = { joined: 0, undone: 0 };
124: 
125:   for (let step = 0; step < 4000; step += 1) {
126:     const roll = rnd();
127:     if (roll < 0.5) {
128:       const a = Math.floor(rnd() * size);
129:       const b = Math.floor(rnd() * size);
130:       const joined = labels[a] !== labels[b];
131:       assert.equal(sets.union(a, b), joined, `union ${a},${b} at step ${step}`);
132:       if (joined) {
133:         const from = labels[b];
134:         const to = labels[a];
135:         labels = labels.map((label) => (label === from ? to : label));
136:         unions += 1;
137:         totals.joined += 1;
138:         history[unions] = labels.slice();
139:       }
140:     } else if (roll < 0.65) {
141:       const token = sets.checkpoint();
142:       assert.equal(token, unions, `checkpoint at step ${step}`);
143:       marks.push(token);
144:     } else if (roll < 0.8 && marks.length > 0) {
145:       const token = marks[Math.floor(rnd() * marks.length)];
146:       totals.undone += unions - token;
147:       assert.equal(sets.rollback(token), unions - token, `rollback to ${token} at step ${step}`);
148:       while (marks.length > 0 && marks[marks.length - 1] > token) marks.pop();
149:       unions = token;
150:       labels = history[unions].slice();
151:     } else if (roll < 0.9) {
152:       const undone = sets.undo();
153:       assert.equal(undone, unions > 0, `undo at step ${step}`);
154:       if (undone) {
155:         unions -= 1;
156:         labels = history[unions].slice();
157:         while (marks.length > 0 && marks[marks.length - 1] > unions) marks.pop();
158:       }
159:     } else {
160:       const a = Math.floor(rnd() * size);
161:       const b = Math.floor(rnd() * size);
162:       const same = labels[a] === labels[b];
163:       assert.deepEqual(
164:         [sets.connected(a, b), sets.find(a) === sets.find(b), sets.sizeOf(a)],
165:         [same, same, labels.filter((label) => label === labels[a]).length],
166:         `probe ${a},${b} at step ${step}`,
167:       );
168:     }
169:     const expected = groupsOf(labels);
170:     assert.deepEqual([sets.components, sets.groups()], [expected.length, expected], `state at step ${step}`);
171:     assert.ok(expected.find((group) => group.includes(0)).includes(sets.find(0)), `root of 0 at step ${step}`);
172:   }
173:   assert.ok(totals.joined > 200 && totals.undone > 100, `expected real history pressure, saw ${JSON.stringify(totals)}`);
174: });

All 10 tests pass. Summary of the fix and final state:

**Root cause of the two failures:** `find()` performed path compression, mutating `#parent` pointers for intermediate nodes that `union()`'s history entries didn't know about. When `undo()`/`rollback()` reversed a union, those extra compressed pointers were left dangling, corrupting the structure.

**Fix:** Removed path compression from `find()`, keeping it a simple walk-to-root. Since union is by size (tree depth stays O(log n)), correctness and adequate performance are preserved, and now every mutation to `#parent`/`#size` is exactly the one recorded in `#history`, making `undo`/`rollback` exact.

Final implementation:
- **`src/dsu.js`**: `checkpoint()` returns `#history.length` (unions performed so far); each `union()` push a record `{attached, root, prevSize}`; `undo()` pops and reverses one record; `rollback(token)` validates the token (safe integer, `0..history.length`) and loops `undo()` until lengths match, returning the count undone.
- **`src/kruskal.js`**: `minimumSpanningForest` validates inputs, sorts edges by `[weight, u, v]`, runs union-find to collect the MST/forest. `componentsWithAlternatives` applies base edges once, checkpoints, then for each alternative applies it, records `components`, and rolls back to the checkpoint before trying the next.

The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

6: /** Infinity, as it appears in a distance map. */
7: const FAR = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
8: 
9: /**
10:  * Deterministic 32-bit PRNG.

13:  */
14: function mulberry32(seed) {
15:   let a = seed >>> 0;

17:     a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) >>> 0;
18:     let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
19:     t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
20:     return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
21:   };
22: }

24: /**
25:  * Computes distances with Bellman-Ford as an independent model.
26:  * @param {Record<string, Record<string, number>>} graph Weighted graph.
27:  * @param {string} source Start node.
28:  * @returns {Record<string, number>} Distance per node.
29:  */
30: function bellmanFord(graph, source) {
31:   const nodes = Object.keys(graph);
32:   const dist = {};
33:   for (const node of nodes) dist[node] = FAR;
34:   dist[source] = 0;
35:   for (let round = 0; round < nodes.length; round += 1) {
36:     for (const node of nodes) {
37:       if (dist[node] === FAR) continue;
38:       for (const [target, weight] of Object.entries(graph[node])) {
39:         if (dist[node] + weight < dist[target]) dist[target] = dist[node] + weight;
40:       }
41:     }
42:   }
43:   return dist;
44: }

52:   island: {},

Finish `src/heap.js` and `src/dijkstra.js`. `IndexedHeap` is a binary min-heap that also keeps an index from key to position, so `push`, `pop`, `remove`, `decreaseKey`, and `setPriority` each run in O(log n) while `has`, `peek`, and `priorityOf` are O(1). The starting point scans a plain array and leaves the keyed operations unimplemented; replace it with the real structure.

Every entry has a string key that is unique within the heap and a finite numeric priority; smaller priorities leave first, and negative and fractional priorities are ordinary. Entries with equal priority leave in the order they were pushed. Each entry is stamped with an insertion number when it is pushed, and that number never changes afterwards, so an entry whose priority is raised and then lowered back still leaves before entries pushed after it. `push(key, priority)` adds an entry; `peek()` returns `{ key, priority }` for the next entry without removing it, and `pop()` removes and returns it; both return `undefined` on an empty heap. `has(key)` and `priorityOf(key)` report what is held. `decreaseKey(key, priority)` lowers a priority, accepting an unchanged one. `setPriority(key, priority)` moves a priority in either direction. `remove(key)` drops any held key and returns whether it did. `drain()` empties the heap and returns every entry in pop order. `size` reports how many entries are held.

`src/dijkstra.js` exports `shortestPaths(graph, source)` and `shortestPath(graph, source, target)` over a weighted directed graph — a plain object mapping each node id to an object of successor ids and weights, each weight a finite number greater than zero. Drive the search with the heap: when a shorter route to a node that is already queued turns up, lower that node's priority in place rather than queueing the node twice. `shortestPaths` returns `{ dist, prev }` covering every node of the graph, with `Infinity` and `null` for a node the source cannot reach. Where several shortest routes to a node tie, `prev` names the smallest predecessor id among them, so the answer never depends on the order nodes came off the queue. `shortestPath` returns `{ distance, path }` with `path` running from source to target, or `null` when the target is unreachable.

A heap key that is not a string raises `TypeError` with message `key must be a string`; a priority that is not a finite number raises `TypeError` with message `priority must be a finite number`; pushing a key that is already held raises `Error` with message `duplicate key: "a"`; re-prioritising a key that is not held raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown key: "a"`; and a `decreaseKey` that would raise a priority raises `RangeError` with message `priority must not increase for "a"`. A graph that is not a non-null, non-array object raises `TypeError` with message `graph must be an object`; a node whose successors are not such an object raises `TypeError` with message `edge map for node "a" must be an object`; an edge or endpoint naming an undeclared node raises `ReferenceError` with message `unknown node: "q"`; a weight that is not a positive finite number raises `RangeError` with message `weight must be positive: "a" -> "b"`; and a non-string source raises `TypeError` with message `source must be a string`. Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Finish the order aggregate in `src/`. `src/index.js` re-exports `STATES`, `COMMAND_TYPES`, `TERMINAL_STATES`, `allowedTypes` and `isTerminal` from `src/machine.js` and `Order` from `src/order.js`; keep that surface. The states are `created`, `paid`, `packed`, `shipped`, `delivered`, `cancelled` and `refunded`; the commands are `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay`, `pack`, `ship`, `deliver`, `cancel` and `refund`. `created` accepts `addItem`, `removeItem`, `pay` and `cancel`; `paid` accepts `pack` and `cancel`; `packed` accepts `ship` and `cancel`; `shipped` accepts `deliver`; `delivered` accepts `refund`; `cancelled` and `refunded` accept nothing and are the terminal states. `allowedTypes(state)` returns that state's commands in ascending order as a fresh array a caller may mutate, and `isTerminal(state)` reports whether the list is empty; both throw `TypeError` with message `unknown state: <state>` for anything else. The exported lists are frozen.

`new Order({ id, createdAt })` starts an order in `created` with no items, nothing paid and nothing refunded. `id` must be a non-empty string and `createdAt`, which defaults to 0, a non-negative integer; violations throw `TypeError` with messages `init must be an object`, `init.id must be a non-empty string` and `init.createdAt must be a non-negative integer`. The read side exposes `id`, `state`, `items` (ascending by sku), `totalCents` (the sum of quantity times unit price), `paidCents`, `refundedCents`, `clockMs`, `shipment`, `deliveredAt`, the `audit` trail and `snapshot()`, which returns `{ id, state, items, totalCents, paidCents, refundedCents, clockMs, seq }` with `seq` the number of audit entries. Every one of these hands back copies: mutating what a getter returned must not change the order.

`apply(command)` runs one command and returns a plain result instead of throwing for business failures. A command carries a `type`, a non-empty `commandId`, a non-negative integer `at`, and the fields its type needs. A structurally malformed command throws `TypeError` and is not recorded: `command must be an object`, `unknown command type: <type>`, `command must carry a non-empty commandId`, `command must carry a non-negative integer at`. Otherwise the checks run in this order, and the first failure decides the outcome. A `commandId` that has been applied before returns exactly the result recorded for it, with `replayed` set to true, and changes nothing at all. An `at` earlier than `clockMs` is rejected with code `'CLOCK_REGRESSION'`, and its audit entry is stamped with the order's current clock so recorded times never decrease; every other command sets `clockMs` to its `at`. A command the current state does not allow is rejected with `'BAD_STATE'`. Then the command's own fields are checked: a missing or empty `sku`, `carrier`, `tracking` or `reason` gives `'MISSING_FIELD'`, and a `qty`, `unitPriceCents` or `amountCents` that is not an integer in range gives `'BAD_AMOUNT'` (`qty` and a refund `amountCents` must be at least 1; `unitPriceCents` and a payment `amountCents` must be at least 0). Then the business guards: adding a sku that is already present gives `'DUPLICATE_SKU'`, removing one that is not gives `'NO_SUCH_ITEM'`, paying an order with no items gives `'EMPTY_ORDER'`, paying anything other than `totalCents` gives `'AMOUNT_MISMATCH'`, and refunding more than `paidCents - refundedCents` gives `'REFUND_TOO_LARGE'`. A successful result is `{ ok: true, state, seq, replayed }` and a rejection is `{ ok: false, code, message, state, seq, replayed }`, where `message` is a non-empty explanation and `seq` is the audit entry number.

Every command that gets as far as the clock check appends exactly one audit entry, whether it succeeded or not: `{ seq, commandId, type, at, from, to, ok }` plus `code` on a rejection, with `seq` counting from 1, `from` the state before and `to` the state after, so a rejection has `from` equal to `to`. Effects: `addItem` and `removeItem` edit the item list and leave the state at `created`; `pay` records `amountCents` as `paidCents` and moves to `paid`; `pack` moves to `packed`; `ship` records the carrier and tracking and moves to `shipped`; `deliver` records `at` as `deliveredAt` and moves to `delivered`; `cancel` refunds everything captured so far and moves to `cancelled`; `refund` adds to `refundedCents` and moves to `refunded` only once the whole payment has been returned. `refundedCents` never exceeds `paidCents`. The static `Order.replay(init, commands)` builds a fresh order and applies each command in turn, giving the same snapshot and audit trail as applying them one at a time; a non-array argument throws `TypeError`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. `src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. The implementation is complete and all tests pass. Summary of the work:

- **`src/tokenize.js`**: Exports `ExprError` and `tokenize`, handling numbers (integer/decimal/exponent forms, including leading-dot decimals), identifiers, single-character operators (`+ - * / % ^`), and punctuation (`( ) ,`), with malformed-number and unexpected-character diagnostics pointing at the correct index.
- **`src/parse.js`**: A precedence-climbing recursive-descent parser (`parseAddSub` → `parseMulDiv` → `parseUnary` → `parseExponent` → `parseAtom`) that produces `number`, `variable`, `unary`, `binary`, and `call` nodes, drops parenthesis nodes, and correctly handles right-associative `^`, tighter-binding unary prefix operators, and function calls with comma-separated argument lists — raising `ExprError` for unexpected end of input, missing closing parens, and unexpected tokens.
- **`src/index.js`**: Re-exports `ExprError`, `tokenize`, `parse`, and implements `evaluate`, walking the tree with a constants table (`pi`, `e`) shadowed by `env` own-properties, a fixed function table (`abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `sign`, `pow`, `atan2`, `min`, `max`) with arity checks, and division/modulo-by-zero and non-finite-result checks pointing at the operator/call index.

`node --test test/*.test.js` reports all 12 tests passing, and `node_modules` does not exist, satisfying both checks in `task.json`. Only files under `src/` were modified; `test/` and `package.json` were left untouched.

goal.objective:
`src/index.js` must export `tokenize`, `parse`, `evaluate` and the error class `ExprError`; how the work is split across files under `src/` is up to you. `tokenize(input)` returns tokens in source order, each `{ type, value, index }` where `index` is the 0-based position in UTF-16 code units. Whitespace separates tokens and is otherwise ignored. The types are `number` (value a JavaScript number), `name` (value the identifier text, matching `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`), `operator` (value one of `+ - * / % ^`), and `lparen`, `rparen`, `comma` whose value is the character. A numeric literal is digits with an optional fractional part, or a leading `.` with digits, each optionally followed by `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digits. Anything that starts like a number but does not fit, including `1.2.3`, `1e`, `4.` and `2abc`, throws `malformed number at 0` pointing at the first character of the literal; any other unusable character throws `unexpected character '$' at 4`, quoting the whole code point.

`parse(input)` returns the expression tree. Nodes are `{ type: 'number', value, index }`, `{ type: 'variable', name, index }`, `{ type: 'unary', op, operand, index }`, `{ type: 'binary', op, left, right, index }` and `{ type: 'call', name, args, index }`; the index of a unary or binary node is its operator's position and the index of a call is its name's position. Parentheses only group, leaving no node of their own. `+` and `-` are left-associative at the lowest precedence, `*`, `/` and `%` are left-associative and bind tighter, a prefix `+` or `-` binds tighter still, and `^` is right-associative and binds tightest, so `-2^2` is -4, `(-2)^2` is 4, `2^3^2` is 512, `2^-2` is 0.25 and `5--3` is 8. A function call is a name immediately followed by a parenthesised, comma-separated argument list, which may be empty.

Failures throw `ExprError` with a 0-based `index` and a message that ends with ` at <index>`: `unexpected end of input at 3` (the index is the input's length), `missing closing parenthesis at 4`, and `unexpected token ')' at 4` quoting the token's source text. Evaluation reports `division by zero at 1` for `/` or `%` with a zero divisor, and `non-finite result at 5` whenever an operation or call produces something that is not a finite number, each pointing at the operator or the call's name.

`evaluate(input, env)` walks the tree in JavaScript double arithmetic and returns a finite number, preserving negative zero. A name resolves first to an own property of `env` and then to the constants `pi` and `e`, so bindings shadow them; an unresolvable name throws `unknown variable: x at 0` and a binding that is not a finite number throws `variable x is not a finite number at 0`. The callable functions are fixed: `abs`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties toward positive infinity), `sign` take exactly one argument; `pow` and `atan2` take exactly two; `min` and `max` take one or more. Calling anything else throws `unknown function: foo at 0`, and a wrong count throws `function abs expects 1 argument, got 2 at 0`, `function pow expects 2 arguments, got 1 at 0` or `function max expects at least 1 argument, got 0 at 0`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root.
